\chapter{Planar Graphs}
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Planar Graphs}

% Generated by scripts/blueprint_from_docstring.py from TCSlib.GraphTheory.Core.PlanarGraphs.
% Prose is extracted from Lean docstrings; verbatim book quotations are excluded.

\begin{definition}[A walk is internally disjoint from a subgraph $H$: no \emph{internal} vertex lies in $H$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Walk.InternallyDisjointFrom}
\label{SimpleGraph.Walk.InternallyDisjointFrom}
\leanok
The walk may start and end on $H$, but between those endpoints it
must stay entirely outside $H$.  This is what makes the bridge relation an
equivalence, and it is why a bridge is a maximal chunk of the graph hanging off
$H$ and touching it only at its attachment points.

\texttt{p.support.tail.dropLast} is the walk's interior --- drop the
first vertex (\texttt{tail}) and the last (\texttt{dropLast}).  \textbf{!} This is \textbf{not} the repo's
\texttt{InternallyDisjoint} (\texttt{TwoConnected.lean:58}), which relates a walk to another
\emph{walk}; here the second argument is a \texttt{Subgraph}.  A walk of length $\le 1$ has empty
interior and so is vacuously internally disjoint from everything --- which is
intended, and is what makes \texttt{bridgeRel} reflexive on single edges.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[B\&M's relation $~$ on $E(G) \ E(H)$: $e_{1} ~ e_{2}$ iff joined by a walk internally disjoint from $H$\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.bridgeRel}
\label{SimpleGraph.bridgeRel}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.InternallyDisjointFrom}
Two edges outside $H$ are related when you can travel from one to the
other without passing through $H$.  Grouping edges into classes carves
$G - E(H)$ into the pieces that hang off $H$ --- those pieces are the bridges.

\texttt{Relation.EqvGen} wraps the book's raw condition in its
reflexive--symmetric--transitive closure, which \emph{discharges} the book's "it is easy
to verify" rather than proving it: whatever the raw relation does, the closure is
an equivalence by construction.  This is a deliberate trade --- the file gains an
equivalence for free, at the cost that \texttt{bridgeRel} is a priori coarser than $\sim$.
It is not actually coarser (the book's $\sim$ really is an equivalence), but nothing
here proves that, so do not appeal to "\texttt{bridgeRel e f} gives a single connecting
walk" --- it gives a \emph{chain} of them.  Several skeletons below rely on this
distinction.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The bridge of $H$ in $G$ containing the edge $e$: the subgraph induced by $e$'s $~$-class]
\lean{SimpleGraph.bridgeOf}
\label{SimpleGraph.bridgeOf}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.bridgeRel}
A bridge is one of the connected pieces remaining when $H$ is
removed, together with the attachment points where it touches $H$.  The three
"immediate" facts quoted above are \texttt{bridgeOf\_connected},
\texttt{exists\_path\_internallyDisjoint} and \texttt{bridge\_inter\_subset\_cycle} below --- none of
them is actually immediate once $\sim$ is a closure.  In planar graph theory bridges
carry the argument: theorem 9.8 says inner bridges of a cycle avoid one another,
theorem 9.9 that a bridge avoiding every outer bridge is transferable, and together
these drive Kuratowski's theorem 9.10.

Indexed by a \emph{representative edge} $e$ rather than by a class,
so "the bridge containing $e$"; two edges give the same bridge exactly when
\texttt{bridgeRel H e f}.  Built with \texttt{Subgraph.mk} directly --- \textbf{not} with
\texttt{SimpleGraph.toSubgraph} (\texttt{Subgraph.lean:559}), which is \emph{spanning} and would put
every vertex of $G$ into every bridge.  Note \texttt{verts} is the union of the class's
edges, so it automatically includes the attachment points.

\textbf{!} Because \texttt{bridgeRel} is reflexive for \emph{any} $e$ (it is an \texttt{EqvGen}), \texttt{bridgeOf H e}
is nonempty even for an $e$ that is not an edge of $G$ at all --- it then has two
vertices and no edges.  Statements about bridges must therefore carry
\texttt{e $\in$ G.edgeSet \textbackslash\{\} H.edgeSet} explicitly.  Two of them below originally omitted it and
were false as a result; both now carry it (see the module header).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Vertices of attachment of the bridge of $e$ to the cycle traced by $c$: $V(B) \cap V(C)$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.attach}
\label{SimpleGraph.attach}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.bridgeOf}
The points at which the bridge touches down onto the cycle.  Almost
everything in \S{}9.4 is a statement about how two bridges' attachment sets interleave
around $C$ --- \texttt{Overlaps}, \texttt{Skew} and the segments below are all built on this one
set.

Specialised to \texttt{H = c.toSubgraph} for a closed walk $c$, since
\S{}9.4 only ever needs bridges of a \emph{cycle}.  A \texttt{Set V}, not a \texttt{Finset}, so that
\texttt{.ncard} is used for $k$ (see theorem 9.6's conclusion).  "$B$ is a $k$-bridge"
is spelled \texttt{(G.attach c e).ncard = k}, and "$B$ and $B'$ are equivalent" is
\texttt{G.attach c e = G.attach c e'}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Position of a vertex along a cycle (index into its support)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Walk.cycleIdx}
\label{SimpleGraph.Walk.cycleIdx}
\leanok
Walking around the cycle from its base point, this records how many
steps it takes to reach $x$.  Comparing indices is how "cyclic order" is expressed
here.

\textbf{!} Mathlib's \texttt{CircularOrder}/\texttt{Btw}/\texttt{SBtw} are order classes on a
\emph{type} and do not apply to the support list of a particular cycle, so they are no
help.  \textbf{!} \texttt{List.idxOf} silently returns the list's \texttt{length} for an absent element,
so every use must be guarded by \texttt{x $\in$ c.support} --- unguarded, all missing vertices
quietly share one position past the end.  Note also that this is genuinely
\emph{linear}, not cyclic: it is measured from $c$'s base point, so \texttt{InCyclicOrder}
below expresses a cyclic condition only up to the choice of that base point.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Four vertices in cyclic order on $c$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Walk.InCyclicOrder}
\label{SimpleGraph.Walk.InCyclicOrder}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.cycleIdx}
Travelling once round the cycle, the four vertices are met in that
order.  This is the configuration making two bridges \emph{skew}: each bridge's two
attachments separate the other's, so drawn inside the same region their connecting
paths would have to cross --- which is precisely the Jordan-curve contradiction in
theorem 9.8.

Rendered as a chain of strict \texttt{cycleIdx} inequalities, i.e. as
a \emph{linear} order from $c$'s base point rather than a genuinely cyclic one.  This is
weaker than the book's phrase: the book's "cyclic order $u, u', v, v'$" is invariant
under rotation, whereas this version distinguishes rotations.  It suffices for
\texttt{Skew}, which existentially quantifies over which attachment plays which role and so
recovers rotation-invariance, but do not reuse \texttt{InCyclicOrder} where genuine
rotation-invariance is needed.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Forward distance along $c$ from $a$ to $x$, in steps, wrapping at the base point]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Walk.cycleDist}
\label{SimpleGraph.Walk.cycleDist}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.cycleIdx}
Stand at $a$ and walk forwards around the cycle; this counts the steps
until $x$ is reached.  Unlike \texttt{cycleIdx} --- which is measured from $c$'s own base
point and so is merely linear --- this is genuinely cyclic: it is what lets an arc
"wrap round" past the base point.

\textbf{!} Guard uses by \texttt{a, x $\in$ c.support}.  \texttt{cycleIdx} returns
\texttt{c.support.length} for an absent vertex, which here yields a meaningless distance.
For $a$ on the cycle the $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction never truncates: \texttt{cycleIdx a $\le$ c.length}
(the base point occurs first at index $0$), so \texttt{cycleIdx x + c.length $\ge$ cycleIdx a}.
The \texttt{\% c.length} is what performs the wraparound; for a degenerate $c$ of length $0$
it is the identity ($n \% 0 = n$ in Lean), which is harmless since every use site
carries \texttt{hc : c.IsCycle}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$x$ lies on the closed arc of $c$ running forwards from $a$ to $b$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Walk.OnArc}
\label{SimpleGraph.Walk.OnArc}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.cycleDist}
Walking forwards from $a$, you meet $x$ no later than $b$.  Both
endpoints count as being on the arc, matching the book's segments, which share their
endpoints with the neighbouring segments and so are edge-disjoint but not
vertex-disjoint.

Stated via \texttt{cycleDist}, so the wraparound is handled: the arc
from $a$ to $b$ may pass through $c$'s base point.  The \texttt{x $\in$ c.support} conjunct is
the guard that keeps vertices off the cycle out, since \texttt{cycleDist} would otherwise
give them a spurious finite distance.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$a$ and $b$ are consecutive vertices of attachment of the bridge of $e$: both are attachments, and no\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ConsecutiveAttach}
\label{SimpleGraph.ConsecutiveAttach}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.OnArc, SimpleGraph.attach}
The arc from $a$ forwards to $b$ is then exactly one \textbf{segment} of the
bridge --- an arc of $C$ with attachments at both ends and none in between.  Ranging
over all consecutive pairs recovers the book's partition of $C$.

"No attachment strictly between" is phrased as: every attachment
on the closed arc is one of the two endpoints.  This is what makes the segments
partition $C$ rather than merely cover it.  The definition does not require the
bridge to have $k \ge 2$ attachments; with fewer, no pair satisfies it, and \texttt{Avoids}
below is then false for want of a witness --- which is the right answer, since a
$0$- or $1$-bridge has no segments to contain anything.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Two bridges of a cycle avoid one another: all the attachments of one lie in a single segment of the other]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Avoids}
\label{SimpleGraph.Avoids}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.ConsecutiveAttach, SimpleGraph.Walk.OnArc, SimpleGraph.attach}
Cut the cycle at one bridge's attachment points, producing arcs; the
two bridges avoid each other when the second's attachments all fall inside a single
arc, so both can be drawn on the same side of $C$ without crossing.

The disjunction mirrors the book's "of one bridge \dots of the
other", which is not symmetric on its face --- the definition says only that \emph{some}
assignment of the two roles works.  A segment of the bridge of $e$ is the arc
\texttt{OnArc a b} for $a$, $b$ consecutive attachments of $e$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Two bridges of a cycle overlap: they do not avoid one another]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Overlaps}
\label{SimpleGraph.Overlaps}
\uses{SimpleGraph.Avoids}
Neither bridge's attachments fit inside a single segment of the other,
so drawn on the same side of $C$ they would be forced to cross.  Theorem 9.8 says
this cannot happen for two inner (or two outer) bridges of a plane graph, and
theorem 9.6 says overlapping comes in only two shapes.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Repaired --- previously \texttt{sorry}.}  This definition formerly had the body
\texttt{Prop := sorry}, making it an \emph{opaque, unspecified} proposition and rendering
\texttt{overlap\_imp\_skew\_or\_equivalent\_three\_bridge} (theorem 9.6) vacuous: with \texttt{Overlaps}
opaque, that theorem said nothing about bridges and "proving" it would have
established nothing.  It also violated the project convention
(\texttt{.claude/CLAUDE.md}): \emph{never \texttt{sorry} in a \texttt{def}} --- a \texttt{sorry}-ed proof is an honest
debt, a \texttt{sorry}-ed definition is a silent change of meaning.

It is now the honest negation of \texttt{Avoids}, built on the segment machinery above
(\texttt{cycleDist} $\to$ \texttt{OnArc} $\to$ \texttt{ConsecutiveAttach} $\to$ \texttt{Avoids}), which is the layer B\&M
assume when they speak of segments.  \textbf{!} \texttt{[DecidableEq V]} had to be added to the
signature, since \texttt{cycleIdx} needs it; every use site already had the instance.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Two bridges of a cycle are skew: they have attachments $a, a', b, b'$ occurring in that cyclic order on\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Skew}
\label{SimpleGraph.Skew}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.InCyclicOrder, SimpleGraph.attach}
The two bridges interleave around the cycle.  In a plane graph this is
fatal for two bridges on the same side: their connecting paths would have to cross,
contradicting the Jordan curve theorem --- which is exactly the (dropped) proof of
theorem 9.8.

The book asks for \emph{four distinct} vertices; the Lean version
requires only $a \ne b$ and $a' \ne b'$.  The remaining distinctness is implied by the
strict \texttt{cycleIdx} chain in \texttt{InCyclicOrder}, since distinct indices force distinct
vertices --- provided all four lie on \texttt{c.support}, which the \texttt{attach} memberships
supply.  Rotation-invariance is recovered by the existential over which attachment
plays which role, compensating for \texttt{InCyclicOrder} being measured from $c$'s base
point.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A longest cycle]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Walk.IsLongestCycle}
\label{SimpleGraph.Walk.IsLongestCycle}
\leanok
A cycle no shorter than any other cycle of $G$.  This is the standard
extremal device: assume the longest cycle is not a Hamilton cycle, then derive a
contradiction from the structure of the bridges hanging off it.  That is exactly how
Chv\'atal--Erd\H{o}s is proved below.

\textbf{!} Not \texttt{girth}/\texttt{egirth}, which are the \emph{shortest} cycle --- the
opposite extremum.  The maximality clause quantifies over cycles at \emph{every} base
point $w$, not just at $u$, which is what makes it a genuine global maximum.  Note
the definition does not assert existence: \texttt{IsLongestCycle} is a hypothesis to be
supplied, and producing one requires knowing $G$ has a cycle at all.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[minDegree\_le\_five\_of\_card\_edge\_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.minDegree_le_five_of_card_edge_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.minDegree_le_five_of_card_edge_le}
\leanok
A planar graph cannot be everywhere dense: Euler's formula caps its
edge count at $3\nu - 6$, so the average degree is below $6$ and some vertex has
degree at most $5$.  This is the fact driving the five-colour theorem 9.11 --- every
planar graph has a vertex of degree at most five to induct on --- and it is why the
arithmetic core was worth salvaging even though the planarity around it was not.

\textbf{!} This is \textbf{not} corollary 9.5.3 as the book states it.
Planarity is replaced by the hypothesis $h\varepsilon$, which corollary 9.5.2 (dropped, being
unstatable without faces) would have supplied.  Ship it under the name
\texttt{minDegree\_le\_five\_of\_card\_edge\_le}, never as \texttt{planar\_minDegree\_le\_five}: the
theorem proved is the arithmetic half only.  Stated additively ($\varepsilon + 6 \le 3\nu$) to
dodge truncated $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction.

Worth knowing while filling: \textbf{\texttt{h$\nu$ : 3 $\le$ Fintype.card V} is unused.}  Steps 1--4
never mention $\nu$ except through the two inequalities $2\varepsilon + 12 \le 6\nu$ and
$6\nu \le 2\varepsilon$, whose contradiction is independent of the size of $\nu$.  The book needs
its $\nu = 1, 2$ caveat because it invokes corollary 9.5.2, which carries $\nu \ge 3$;
once that corollary is replaced by the raw hypothesis $h\varepsilon$, the caveat evaporates.
$h\nu$ is kept only so the statement still reads as the book's; do not go looking for
a place to use it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[card\_edgeFinset\_add\_card\_edgeFinset\_compl]
\lean{SimpleGraph.card_edgeFinset_add_card_edgeFinset_compl}
\label{SimpleGraph.card_edgeFinset_add_card_edgeFinset_compl}
\leanok
$\varepsilon(G) + \varepsilon(G^{c}) = C(\nu, 2)$.

Every unordered pair of distinct vertices carries an edge in exactly
one of $G$ and $G^{c}$ --- that is precisely what complementation means --- so the two
edge counts partition the $C(\nu, 2)$ available pairs.  Together with the planar edge
bound applied to \emph{both} graphs, this is the whole of exercise 9.3.3(a).

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits at the time of writing; step 3 is
the part most likely to exist already, so search before building).  Needs both
\texttt{DecidableRel G.Adj} and \texttt{DecidableRel G$^{c}$.Adj} as instances, since \texttt{edgeFinset} is
only available with decidable adjacency.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[not\_both\_card\_edge\_le\_of\_eleven\_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.not_both_card_edge_le_of_eleven_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.not_both_card_edge_le_of_eleven_le}
\leanok
Planarity forces sparsity, and a graph and its complement cannot both
be sparse: between them they must carry \emph{every} possible edge, and $C(\nu,2)$ outgrows
$2(3\nu-6)$ at exactly $\nu = 11$.  Part (b) of the exercise confirms the bound is
sharp in spirit --- there is a simple planar graph on $\nu = 8$ vertices whose
complement is also planar.

\textbf{!} This is \textbf{not} exercise 9.3.3(a) as stated.  "Planar" is
replaced by the corollary-9.5.2 edge bound on \emph{both} sides, so what is proved is
that the two bounds are jointly unsatisfiable --- the arithmetic obstruction, with
the topology stripped out.  The conclusion is therefore a negated conjunction
rather than "$G^{c}$ is nonplanar".
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[bridge\_inter\_subset\_cycle]
\lean{SimpleGraph.bridge_inter_subset_cycle}
\label{SimpleGraph.bridge_inter_subset_cycle}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.bridgeOf, SimpleGraph.bridgeRel}
Bridges can only meet on $H$ itself.  If a vertex outside $H$ lay in
two bridges, edges of both would meet there, and a walk through it from one to the
other stays outside $H$ --- so those edges are related and the two bridges were the
same class all along.  This is what makes the bridge decomposition genuinely a
decomposition: the bridges partition $E(G) \ E(H)$ and meet only at attachment
points.

"Distinct bridges" is \texttt{hne : $\lnot$ G.bridgeRel H e e'} --- two
representative edges in different classes --- rather than a disequality of subgraphs,
which would be weaker and harder to use.  The hypotheses $he$, $he'$ placing both
edges in \texttt{G.edgeSet \textbackslash\{\} H.edgeSet} are present and are needed: without them
\texttt{bridgeOf} degenerates (see its docstring).
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[bridgeOf\_connected]
\lean{SimpleGraph.bridgeOf_connected}
\label{SimpleGraph.bridgeOf_connected}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.bridgeOf}
A bridge is one connected lump: its edges all lie in one $\sim$-class,
and $\sim$ relates edges precisely when a walk avoiding $H$'s interior joins them.

Together with \texttt{exists\_path\_internallyDisjoint} this is one of
two facts B\&M wave through and that everything downstream (theorems 9.6, 9.7 and
exercise 9.4.3) actually consumes.  Step 3 is the real content and is worth
extracting as a lemma about \texttt{bridgeRel} chains, since the same induction is needed
for the companion result.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_path\_internallyDisjoint]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_path_internallyDisjoint}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_path_internallyDisjoint}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.InternallyDisjointFrom, SimpleGraph.bridgeOf}
Not only is a bridge connected, but the connection can be made without
re-entering $H$.  This is the form actually used downstream: theorem 9.7 needs
$(v_{1},v_{2})$-paths inside a bridge avoiding the cycle internally, and the dropped
theorem 9.8 needs the same to reach its Jordan-curve contradiction.

The path is asked for as a \texttt{G.Walk}, not a walk in the bridge.
That is equivalent and more convenient: a walk in $G$ between two bridge vertices
that is internally disjoint from $H$ automatically has all its edges in the bridge's
class.  Note the trans case in step 1 is the reason this is genuinely harder than
\texttt{bridgeOf\_connected} and not a corollary of it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[bridge\_tripod\_of\_three\_attachments]
\lean{SimpleGraph.bridge_tripod_of_three_attachments}
\label{SimpleGraph.bridge_tripod_of_three_attachments}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.bridgeOf}
The picture is a \textbf{tripod}: a hub $v_{0}$ strictly off the cycle, with
three legs reaching down to the three attachment points.  This is what the dropped
theorem 9.8 uses to dispose of equivalent 3-bridges, and what Kuratowski's theorem
9.10 uses to locate $K_{3,3}$ subdivisions.

The "only the vertex $v_{0}$ in common" conditions are spelled as
three \texttt{$\forall$ x, x $\in$ \_.support $\to$ x $\in$ \_.support $\to$ x = v$_{0}$} clauses rather than as set
equalities, which is what the \texttt{takeUntil}/\texttt{dropUntil} lemmas deliver directly.
Note step 5 is genuinely extra work: the book states $v_{0} \in V(B) \ V(C)$ in the
theorem but never justifies it in the proof.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[overlap\_imp\_skew\_or\_equivalent\_three\_bridge]
\lean{SimpleGraph.overlap_imp_skew_or_equivalent_three_bridge}
\label{SimpleGraph.overlap_imp_skew_or_equivalent_three_bridge}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Overlaps, SimpleGraph.Skew, SimpleGraph.attach}
Overlapping comes in exactly two flavours.  This dichotomy is what the
dropped theorem 9.8 disposes of --- the skew case by the Jordan curve theorem, the
equivalent-3-bridge case by the tripod of theorem 9.7.  It is the reason theorem 9.7
exists at all.

"Equivalent 3-bridges" is rendered as the conjunction
\texttt{attach c e = attach c e' $\land$ (attach c e).ncard = 3}, matching the book's definition
of equivalent $k$-bridges.  Steps 2--4 all reduce to arc arithmetic on \texttt{cycleIdx},
so the segment machinery built for \texttt{Overlaps} will carry most of them.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_bridge\_off\_longest\_cycle]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_bridge_off_longest_cycle}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_bridge_off_longest_cycle}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.IsLongestCycle, SimpleGraph.bridgeOf}
Since $G$ is not hamiltonian the longest cycle misses some vertex;
connectivity joins that vertex to the cycle, and the joining path's edges lie in a
bridge that therefore reaches off $C$.  This is the setup for the whole exercise ---
that bridge is the object whose attachments part (ii) constrains, and Chv\'atal--Erd\H{o}s
falls out of those constraints.

Note this is the \emph{only} one of the three 9.4.3 statements that
carries \texttt{hnh}; part (ii) as stated below drops it, which is where its defect comes
from.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[succ\_attachments\_not\_adj]
\lean{SimpleGraph.succ_attachments_not_adj}
\label{SimpleGraph.succ_attachments_not_adj}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.IsLongestCycle, SimpleGraph.attach, SimpleGraph.bridgeOf}
The successors of a bridge's attachment points form an *independent
set*.  That is exactly the leverage Chv\'atal--Erd\H{o}s needs: a bridge with many
attachments yields a large independent set, which $\alpha \le \kappa$ forbids.

Indices are into the walk (\texttt{c.getVert i}), so $i + 1$ is the
successor along $c$; the wraparound at the end of the support is handled by
\texttt{getVert} saturating, which is why step 3 must be phrased as two explicit arcs
rather than as index arithmetic mod $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[chvatal\_erdos\_hamiltonian]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chvatal_erdos_hamiltonian}
\label{SimpleGraph.chvatal_erdos_hamiltonian}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.vertexConnectivity}
$\alpha$ is the independence number and $\kappa$ the connectivity, so the
hypothesis says the graph is at least as well connected as it is "spread out".  This
is one of the most elegant sufficient conditions for hamiltonicity known, and the
whole bridge apparatus of \S{}9.4 that survives in this file exists to reach it --- it is
the prize of the surviving combinatorial core.

\textbf{!} \texttt{h$\nu$ : 3 $\le$ Fintype.card V} is \textbf{load-bearing} and is \emph{not} in
B\&M --- the statement is false without it.  $K_{2}$ has $\alpha = 1$ and $\kappa = 1$, so $\alpha \le \kappa$
holds, yet $K_{2}$ has no Hamilton cycle, there being no cycle of length two.  ($K_{1}$ is
similar.)  Step 5 is where most of the work sits; step 4's cut argument is the part
most likely to need its own supporting lemma.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[lineGraph\_colorable\_three\_of\_isHamiltonian\_of\_three\_regular]
\lean{SimpleGraph.lineGraph_colorable_three_of_isHamiltonian_of_three_regular}
\label{SimpleGraph.lineGraph_colorable_three_of_isHamiltonian_of_three_regular}
\leanok
A cubic hamiltonian graph splits into an even cycle plus a perfect
matching; two colours alternate around the cycle and the third takes the matching.

\emph{Why this matters (\S{}9.7).}  Tait (1880) showed the four-colour conjecture equivalent
to "every simple 3-regular 3-connected planar graph has a Tait colouring" (theorem
9.12(iii)), and then \emph{by mistakenly assuming that every such graph is hamiltonian},
gave a "proof" of the conjecture using exactly this exercise.  Over half a century
later Tutte (1946) exhibited a nonhamiltonian 3-regular 3-connected planar graph,
invalidating the argument.  So this exercise is sound; only Tait's extra assumption
was not.

A Tait colouring is spelled \texttt{G.lineGraph.Colorable 3}, needing
no new definitions --- \texttt{lineGraph} has the edges of $G$ as vertices, adjacent when
they share an end, so a proper colouring of it \emph{is} a proper edge colouring of $G$.
Step 3's parity assignment is the fiddly part: it needs a function from an edge of
$c$ to its index along $c$, which \texttt{c.edges} provides as a list position.
\end{theorem}
